opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because there's a real tension in it. On one hand, we're in an unusual position. We see a lot of what people try to do with the models, and we have a sense of what the models are actually capable of, which is often ahead of what people are using them for. So there's a capability overhang, and part of our job is to close that gap and show people what's possible.

On the other hand, we don't want to be the company that builds every application and crowds everyone out. The ecosystem is where most of the value will get created. There are so many domains, like legal, healthcare, finance, education, and specific kinds of software work, where the people building on top of us have deep context we'll never have. They know the workflows, the customers, and the edge cases. If we tried to do all of that ourselves, we'd do it worse, and we'd also make developers nervous about building on our platform.

So the way I think about it is that we should build things that are horizontal and that teach people something. Claude Code is a good example. Coding was a place where we had strong internal conviction, because our own engineers were using it constantly. By putting out a product there, we didn't just serve that use case. We showed the world what an agentic model can do when you give it real tools and let it run for a while. A lot of people building agents in completely unrelated domains took lessons from that.

The other piece is making the primitives really good and really open: things like tool use, the Model Context Protocol, and the agent SDK. Those are infrastructure, not apps. The goal is to lower the cost for anyone to build something ambitious. If we do our jobs well, the most surprising and valuable uses of the models won't come from us at all. They'll come from some small team that saw a problem we didn't even know existed.

And then there's just listening. A lot of what we've learned about what the models are good for has come from customers telling us, "Hey, we tried this weird thing and it worked." Our job is to notice those moments, make them work better, and help other people find them faster.

r001.rationale: The response says Anthropic should show what models can do and lower the cost of building with open primitives, but it does not state that easy hands-on access to the models helps people discover uses.

r002.rationale: The response describes MCP as an open infrastructure primitive, but does not present it as an alternative to integrations limited to each provider’s bespoke partnerships.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a tension there that we think about a lot. On one hand, we have this product surface, Claude.ai, and we learn an enormous amount from it. We see what people are actually trying to do, where the model falls down, what delights people. That feedback loop is really valuable for making the models better. On the other hand, we don't want to be in a position where we're competing with the developers who are building on our API, because the whole point is that the ecosystem should be bigger than anything we could build ourselves.

So the way I think about it is that our job is mostly to show what's possible and then get out of the way. A lot of the most interesting use cases we've seen weren't things we predicted. People use the models for legal document review, for coding, for customer support, for drug discovery workflows, for all kinds of things we'd never have had the bandwidth to build products around. What we can do is publish really good documentation, show people prompting techniques, give them things like the cookbook and example code, and make the pricing and rate limits sane so that people can experiment without a huge upfront commitment.

The other piece is that I think the frontier is moving so fast that the right way to discover uses is to just put the model in front of people and let them try stuff. Every time we ship a new model, people find things it can do that we didn't know about. So keeping that surface area open, whether through the API, through partners like Amazon and Google, or through the consumer product, matters more than us trying to be prescriptive about use cases.

And honestly, when we do build first-party things, I'd like them to be focused on areas where we have some unique advantage, like safety features, or where there's a gap nobody else is filling. If a developer is doing something well, we should be cheering for them and making the model better for them, not trying to eat their lunch.

r001.rationale: The response says to put models in front of people so they can try them, and describes accessible API experimentation through sane pricing and rate limits.

r002.rationale: The response mentions the API and partners such as Amazon and Google, but does not present MCP as an alternative to provider-specific integrations.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a balance between showing people what’s possible and leaving room for them to surprise us. You can put a powerful model in front of someone, but a blank text box doesn’t necessarily help them understand how it fits into their life or their work. So we should make that first useful experience easier—with concrete examples and products that help people develop an intuition for what the model can do.

At the same time, we’re not going to imagine every valuable application ourselves. Developers and people who deeply understand a particular field will find uses we wouldn’t think of. Our job is to give them capable models, tools that are easy to build with, and a reason to feel confident investing in the platform.

Those two things can reinforce each other. When people discover something useful through our products, they start asking where else they could use it. That creates opportunities for the ecosystem, and what people build teaches us where the models need to get better.

r001.rationale: The response says putting a capable model in front of people and making the first useful experience easier helps them understand what it can do and where it fits.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention MCP or present it as an alternative to provider-specific bespoke partnerships.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should do two things. One is help people get a feel for what the models can do. A blank text box asks a lot of you—you have to imagine the use case, figure out how to ask for it, and decide whether the result is good. Concrete examples can make that much easier, especially examples that connect to work people already do.

The other is leave room for developers to discover things we wouldn’t think of. We shouldn’t assume we know every useful application. We want to build capable models, make them easy to build with, and learn from the people using them.

There’s a balance there. Building products ourselves helps us understand the experience and where the models fall short. But we also want an ecosystem where someone with deep knowledge of a particular problem can build something really valuable. Ideally, what we do makes that opportunity bigger.
